problem: The chapter states that contiguous allocation suffers both kinds of fragmentation but 'linked allocation suffers neither in data blocks'. Linked allocation does avoid external fragmentation, but the last block of a linked file can still be only partly filled, so fixed-size blocks leave internal fragmentation there too. A student will write 'linked has no internal fragmentation' and lose marks.
fix: Contiguous allocation suffers both: internal waste in the last block and external gaps between runs. Linked allocation suffers no external fragmentation, but its last block can still hold unused space (internal fragmentation), the same as any fixed-block scheme. Indexed allocation likewise has no external fragmentation, though its index block and its last data block can both be partly unused.

problem: The Index row has five cells ('30' plus four data blocks) while the other rows have four, and show_index labels columns 0 to 4. So logical block 2 appears in column 2 for Contig and Linked but in column 3 for Index, and the emphasised cells do not line up down the table. The marks are correct per cell, but the picture misleads.
fix: Keep the index block 30 out of the row of data blocks (put it in the row label, for example 'Index (30)'), so every row has exactly four cells 0 to 3 and column 2 shows 14, 20, 20 with the accent on the same column.

problem: 'one entry per disk block' is not exact for FAT: the table has one entry per cluster, and a cluster is one or more blocks/sectors. A student may write that FAT entries map 1:1 with disk blocks.
fix: Say the FAT keeps one entry per allocation unit, which is a cluster of one or more blocks; the entry holds the next cluster number of the chain, and an end-of-file value marks the last cluster.
